registers.role: sample frame; treatment construction (original nominal purchase price R), outcome construction (realized sale price P), and the tax assessor valuation used in the hedonic model
variables_mentioned: tax assessor valuation of the property

registers.role: controls / hedonic characteristics of the housing stock and the sample frame for the extensive margin
variables_mentioned: number of rooms, bathrooms and showers
unoccupied at the time of sale or retraction
distance to the nearest major city

registers.name_in_paper: Property listings data provided by RealView
registers.role: treatment/outcome: initial listing price L, listing dates and time on the market; 79.6 percent of all sale transactions have associated listing data

registers.name_in_paper: Mortgage data from the Danish central bank (Danmarks Nationalbank), collected from mortgage banks
registers.role: treatment construction: outstanding mortgage balance M used to build potential home equity
linkage: individual identifiers (CPR) and the family identification number linking members of the same household

registers.name_in_paper: Official records at SKAT on individual income and wealth
registers.role: controls: household wealth and income, including net financial assets available for a down payment
data access and flagging of anomalous or extreme-price transactions
variables_mentioned: flag for anomalous or unusual transaction

linkages: RealView listings linked to the cleaned and filtered sale transactions in the official property registers; 79.6 percent of all sale transactions have associated listing data, with unmatched transactions generally occurring off market as direct private transfers

All mortgages attached to each property (Danmarks Nationalbank) matched to the property; where several mortgages are outstanding for the same property they are summed and a weighted average interest rate and LTV ratio is calculated
Properties matched to the owner ID and the owner's household ID so that housing transactions can be linked to wealth and income data
Individual demographic, income and wealth records linked by CPR number and aggregated to the household level using the family identification number
Listings and the full housing stock linked to the hedonic predicted price P̂ estimated on sold listings

sample.universe: All registered properties in Denmark and their transactions, 1992-2016, with property listings 2008-2016 and mortgage data 2009-2016; restricted to normal residential owner-occupied housing
sample.unit_of_observation: property listing (main sample); property-year (housing stock / extensive margin sample); municipality-year (price-volume regression); municipality (demand concavity exercises)
selection_rules: transactions for which both nominal losses and home equity can be measured
properties bought during or after 1992, so that the purchase price (the reference price R) is observed
years 2009-2016, the period for which mortgage data are available
properties for which both the owner ID and the owner's household ID are known
exclude properties with a registered size of zero
exclude properties sold at unusually high or low prices (below 100,000 DKK and above 20 million DKK in 2015, or marked as having an extreme price by Statistics Denmark)

for listings ending in a final sale, drop within-family transactions, transactions flagged as anomalous or unusual by Statistics Denmark, and transactions where the buyer is the government, a company or an organization
restrict to normal residential housing, dropping summer houses
drop listings from households that own more than three properties in total
sample.n_observations: 214,103 listings (70.4 percent sold, 29.6 percent retracted), of which 172,225 have an attached mortgage and 41,878 have none; housing stock dataset of 5,538,052 property-year observations
sample.n_individuals: 191,507 unique households and 178,933 unique properties in the listing sample; 807,345 unique properties in the housing stock dataset

construction_notes: Listing premium ℓ = ln L − ln P̂, where L is the reported initial listing price and P̂ comes from the hedonic model; mean ℓ is 12.1 percent and ℓ > 0 for 74 percent of the sample
Potential gains Ĝ = ln P̂ − ln R with R the nominal purchase price; mean Ĝ is 38 percent and 23 percent of property-years exhibit negative gains

Potential home equity Ĥ = ln P̂ − ln M with M the outstanding mortgage balance; mean 41 percent, median 37 percent; 35 percent of sellers potentially face a binding constraint (Ĥ < 20 percent); the modal Ĥ conditional on having a mortgage is around 18 percent

Hedonic pricing model, equation (6): ln(P_it) = ξ_tm + β_ft 1_{i=f} + β_x X_it + β_fx 1_{i=f} X_it + Φ(v_it) + 1_{i=f} Φ(v_it) + ε_it, with year-by-municipality fixed effects (98 municipalities) and a third-order polynomial, including a square-root term, of the previous-year tax assessor valuation; R² = 0.88 in the full sample (0.85 in levels, 0.77 without the tax assessor valuation)

A model period is six months; α(ℓ) is the probability the transaction completes within six months of listing, derived from time on the market, which is winsorized at 200 weeks; mean (median) TOM is 35 (24) weeks; α(ℓ) is smoothed with a generalized logistic function whose lower bound is restricted to zero
β(ℓ) = β0 + β1 ℓ estimated in the data with β0 = −0.083 and β1 = 0.865; the dispersion σ(ℓ) of realizations around β(ℓ) is fitted with a third-degree polynomial of ℓ
The hedonic value P̂ is normalized to one in the model, so all model quantities are expressed in units of P̂, and premia map to log differences

Moments are binned averages in 1 percentage point bins of potential gains, potential home equity or realized gains over the interval [−40, +40] percent (79 bins each); the full moment vector has 79 × 7 = 474 elements
The counterfactual distribution for bunching is the empirical frequency of realized sales in each 1 percentage point bin of potential gains ln P̂ − ln R

Municipalities (98 in Denmark, about 60,000 inhabitants and roughly 1,800 listings each) are grouped into bottom 5 percent, middle 90 percent and top 5 percent by the slope of α(ℓ) for ℓ ∈ [0, 40]; the exercise is cross-checked using shires (about 80 listings each)
The down-payment fraction γ is calibrated at 20 percent, matching the Danish Mortgage Act limit of 80 percent LTV at issuance
Standard errors come from a bootstrap that redraws the underlying data clustered at the shire level and re-estimates P̂, the moments, α(ℓ), β(ℓ) and the structural parameters in each draw
The conditional variance of Ĝ given Ĥ is 0.255 and of Ĥ given Ĝ is 0.130
The unconditional average annual listing propensity is 3.91 percent of the housing stock (between 3 and 4.5 percent across sample years)

claims.statement: In Table 2 model variant 1 of the structural model of Danish house-selling decisions, the reference dependence parameter η is estimated at 0.34.

treatment.label: Realized nominal gain G(ℓ) = P(ℓ) − R relative to the original nominal purchase price

register_source.value: SKAT property transaction register and the Danish housing register (Bygnings-og Boligregisteret): original nominal purchase price R, 1992-2016; no DST variable name is given

definition.value: Realized gain of the sale over the reference price R, which the paper sets to the original nominal purchase price of the property; in the data computed as ln P − ln R and expressed in units of the hedonic value P̂, which is normalized to one in the model.

timing.value: R is the price at the household's purchase of the property (1992 or later); G is realized at the sale, 2009-2016

outcome.label: Seller's utility from the house sale, u(P(ℓ),R)

definition.value: Piecewise-linear utility over the realized sale price and realized nominal gains, equation (3) (equation (7) when the preference notch is included), expressed in units of the hedonic property value P̂, which is normalized to one.

timing.value: evaluated at the realized sale in period 1 of the model

units.value: dimensionless weight on realized nominal gains in seller utility, relative to a weight of one on the final sale price

estimand.target_population: Danish owner-occupiers listing a property for sale in 2009-2016, assumed to share the same preference parameters across locations

population.description: Danish owner-occupied housing listings, 2009-2016, for properties bought in or after 1992 (so the nominal purchase price is observed) and merged to mortgage and household financial data; the extensive-margin moments use the full Danish housing stock filtered in the same way
subgroups_defined: municipality groups by the concavity of demand: bottom 5 percent, middle 90 percent, top 5 percent
listings with an attached mortgage (172,225) versus listings with no mortgage (41,878)
population.selection: Listings of normal residential owner-occupied housing whose property was bought during or after 1992 and whose owner and household IDs are known; foreclosures, zero-size properties, extreme prices (below 100,000 DKK and above 20 million DKK in 2015), within-family transactions, transactions flagged as anomalous, transactions with corporate, government or organizational buyers, summer houses, and listings by households owning more than three properties are excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across 214,103 Danish listings in potential gains Ĝ = ln P̂ − ln R and potential home equity Ĥ = ln P̂ − ln M, the distribution of realized gains around zero, the listing propensity of the housing stock across potential gains, and cross-municipality variation in the concavity of demand

key_assumptions.assumption: The seller's reference price R is the original nominal purchase price of the property.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pronounced bunching of realized sales precisely at G = 0 in Figure 6, which the paper calls nonparametric empirical support for this choice of R, plus robustness of the bunching to round numbers, holding periods and the level of R (online Appendix J.1).

key_assumptions.assumption: Seller preferences are the same across locations, so variation in listing behaviour across municipalities that is unexplained by differences in demand concavity identifies loss aversion.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 9 shows that the model reproduces the listing-premium profiles of the three municipality groups.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sellers take the distribution of negotiation outcomes as given: the demand functions α(ℓ) and β(ℓ) are estimated from the data and are exogenous to sellers' decisions and preferences in the model.

Targeting ability is a fixed feature of each seller type: a fraction π of sellers target the final price precisely and the remainder draw a random realization from the estimated distribution B(0, σ(ℓ)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper points to strict bunching precisely at the reference point (precise targeters) alongside evidence of extensive negotiation with uncertain outcomes (imprecise targeters).

key_assumptions.assumption: The hedonic model (6) recovers the expected house value P̂, so that measured listing premia and measured potential gains are not generated by unobserved, time-varying property quality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Alternative hedonic specifications (renovation expenses, repeat sales I and II) and simulated de-biasing of P̂ under conservative, moderate and aggressive unobserved quality, all reported in Table 3; the paper argues that unobserved quality biases listing premia and β(ℓ) in offsetting directions.

key_assumptions.assumption: The required down-payment fraction γ is calibrated at 20 percent rather than estimated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The Danish Mortgage Act restricts LTV at issuance by mortgage banks to 80 percent or lower over the whole sample period.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on properties bought during or after 1992 (so that the nominal purchase price R is observed) and on 2009-2016, the years for which mortgage data exist.

implies_edges.from: Property bought in or after 1992 with mortgage data in 2009-2016

threats_discussed: unobserved, potentially time-varying property quality biasing the hedonic value P̂ and hence measured potential gains and listing premia
idiosyncratic over- or underpayment by the seller at the point of purchase
concave demand generating an asymmetric listing-premium schedule even with symmetric preferences, a confound for loss aversion
imprecise targeting of final prices making λ not uniquely identified by the hockey stick when π < 1
selection into listing (the extensive margin) driving observed intensive-margin listing premia
bunching at round numbers, holding-period heterogeneity and heterogeneity in the reference price R
robustness_checks: alternative hedonic models for P̂: renovation expenses, repeat sales I and repeat sales II (Table 3)
simulated de-biasing of P̂ for seller-known unobserved quality at conservative, moderate and aggressive levels (Table 3)
inverse-variance weighting matrix W = V^-1 instead of the identity matrix (Table 3)
bunching robust to excluding up to 20 percent of observations at round numbers, to splits by holding period and to quintiles of the reference price R (online Appendix J.1)
regression kink design for the listing premium hockey stick (online Appendix I.6)
varying the six-month window used for α(ℓ) to 3, 9 or 12 months
unresolved_confounders: the interaction between down-payment constraints and reference dependence: the model cannot rationalize the attenuation of reference dependence among financially constrained sellers

treatment.label: Successful sale and move in period 1 (receipt of the moving shock θ)

definition.value: The 'moving shock' θ ∼ N(θm, θσ) is a boost to lifetime utility that the seller receives only in the event of a successful sale and move; θm is its mean. It is recovered as a latent variable, not measured in a register.

timing.value: received in period 1 of the two-period model, conditional on a completed sale

outcome.label: Average value of the moving shock θm (boost to lifetime utility from a successful sale and move)

definition.value: Mean of the normal distribution of the moving shock θ, expressed in units of the hedonic property value P̂; the paper reinterprets the distribution of θ as conditional on the small fraction of the stock that is listed each year.

timing.value: lifetime utility discounted to the present at the time of the listing decision

units.value: units of the hedonic property value P̂ (P̂ normalized to one)

evidence.annotation: The figure reports the model fit for conditional listing premia profiles, conditioning on different levels of home equity and potential gains. The model is evaluated at the set of parameters estimated for the complete set of empirical moments, as indicated in row 8 of Table 2. In panel B, we report the estimated slope of the listing premium along the potential gains and home equity dimension, respectively, measured in subsamples that correspond to the interval of the conditioning variable shown on the horizontal axis. Error bars indicate 99 percent confidence intervals for each point estimate.
